question.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}}=\frac{2\cdot 0\cdot {0}^{3}}{{0}^{6}+8\cdot {0}^{2}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{6}+8{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{2}({x}^{4}+8)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}+8} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{3},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{3}}\,\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{6}}{{x}^{6}+8{x}^{6}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{6}}{9{x}^{6}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2y{x}^{3}}{{x}^{6}+8{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$
